title: John Cusack Becomes First Hollywood Star to Back India's CJP Protests
excerpt: The actor shared an Arundhati Roy essay and called her his 'favourite fellow cockroach,' extending the Jantar Mantar movement's reach to international audiences for the first time from a Western celebrity.
body:
• John Cusack is the first major Western celebrity to support the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests in India.
  • Cusack shared a link to an essay by Indian author Arundhati Roy, highlighting his connection to the movement.
  • The term 'cockroach' has been embraced by India's Gen Z protesters as a symbol of defiance against derogatory remarks from officials.
  • Cusack's support comes after a significant protest where thousands demanded accountability from the Indian government over exam irregularities.

Hollywood actor John Cusack on Wednesday became the first major Western celebrity to publicly voice support for the student-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests that have gripped India for weeks. The High Fidelity star posted on X, sharing a link to an essay by Indian author Arundhati Roy titled "Cockroach Democracy: Unarmed and Dangerous," published in The Wire.

https://x.com/CNNnews18/status/2080176429044797872

"Beautiful news from my favorite fellow cockroach," Cusack wrote, embracing the label that India's Gen Z protesters have turned from an insult into a badge of defiance.

A Bond Forged in Dissent

The word "fellow" was no accident. Cusack and Roy have been close friends and intellectual collaborators for over a decade. In 2013, the two traveled together to Moscow along with Pentagon Papers whistleblower Daniel Ellsberg to meet Edward Snowden, an encounter they documented in their co-authored book Things That Can and Cannot Be Said.

"She can disarm you at any time with her friendly hustler's grin, but her eyes see things and love things so fiercely, it's frightening at times."

— John Cusack, writing about Arundhati Roy

By calling Roy his "favourite fellow cockroach," Cusack placed himself squarely within the movement's symbolic universe — the satirical political identity born when Chief Justice of India Surya Kant compared unemployed youth to "cockroaches" during a court hearing in May. Within days of that remark, 30-year-old Abhijeet Dipke founded the CJP, and millions of young Indians claimed the slur as their own under the hashtag #MainBhiCockroach.

Post-Crackdown Solidarity

Cusack's post arrived three days after the CJP's most dramatic confrontation with authorities yet. On July 20, thousands of supporters attempted a "Chalo Sansad" march from Jantar Mantar toward Parliament, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET-UG paper leak scandal and broader exam irregularities. Delhi Police deployed tear gas and baton charges to disperse the crowd, with protest organisers claiming 150 demonstrators were injured. Police reported 118 officers hurt and roughly 70 protesters detained.

The clashes triggered a wave of celebrity support domestically. Actors Shabana Azmi and Prakash Raj physically joined the Jantar Mantar demonstrations, while Diljit Dosanjh, Sonakshi Sinha, Bhumi Pednekar, Vir Das, Anurag Kashyap, Preity Zinta, and Twinkle Khanna voiced solidarity on social media. Comedians Abish Mathew and influencer Ayesha Khan were reportedly detained. But until Cusack's post, no prominent Western figure had weighed in.

Not His First Time Speaking Up for India

The 60-year-old actor's engagement with Indian politics is not new. In December 2019, during protests against the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), Cusack tweeted about police action against students at Delhi's Jamia Millia Islamia University, writing: "Reports from Delhi are it was a war zone last night — Fascism is not a joke — we use the word with the understanding it's deadly."

He shared Roy's work then too, posting her commentary alongside video from the Jamia campus and writing about "fascists in India trying to set students against each other." In 2022, he supported Congress leader Rahul Gandhi's Bharat Jodo Yatra, posting "solidarity to all anti-fascists everywhere."

"Reports from Delhi are it was a war zone last night — Fascism is not a joke — we use the word with the understanding it's deadly."

— John Cusack, during 2019 CAA protests

International Spotlight on Jantar Mantar

Cusack's endorsement adds to growing international media attention on the protests. The New York Times, The Guardian, The Times of London, and Al Jazeera have all carried substantial coverage of the CJP movement in recent days. The Times reported that the July 20 confrontation was "one of the most serious yet in the youth-led movement's campaign."

For the Indian diaspora, the Hollywood actor's intervention carries particular resonance. Many NRIs have followed the CJP movement closely on social media, and Cusack's post — viewed widely across platforms — lends the protests a cross-cultural legitimacy that domestic celebrity endorsements alone may not achieve.

What Comes Next

The CJP has called for nationwide protests on Friday, July 24, with demonstrations planned across multiple cities. Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced fast-track courts to try paper leak cases, and Health Minister JP Nadda agreed to meet CJP spokesperson Saurav Das — the first direct engagement between the government and the movement's leadership. Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk, who has been on a hunger strike in solidarity with the students, remains at Safdarjung Hospital under what he has described as restricted movement.

Whether Cusack's statement marks the beginning of broader Western celebrity engagement with India's youth protests or remains a one-off remains to be seen. But for the cockroaches of Jantar Mantar, the message from across the Pacific was clear: the world is, in fact, watching.
